planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; registered in 1929 by Arlow Stout, Mikado was the first daylily cultivar bred with a distinct contrasting band of color in the throat, a trait now called an eyezone.

directions: Introduced in 1929 by daylily hybridizer Arlow Stout at the New York Botanical Garden, Mikado holds a landmark place in daylily history as the first cultivar bred with a distinct mahogany-red band ringing its orange throat, a patterned trait breeders now call an eyezone. That single innovation opened an entirely new direction for hybridizers and underlies the eyed and banded daylilies common in gardens today, making Mikado a genuine foundation stone of modern daylily breeding rather than just an old curiosity. The clump produces sturdy scapes of medium-sized, boldly contrasting flowers over a long midsummer season and has proven durable enough to remain in circulation for nearly a century. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Dauntless Daylily (Historic Stout Medal Pastel Trumpet Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in 1935 by Arlow Stout, Dauntless helped pioneer the broader-petaled, flatter flower form that came to define modern daylily breeding and later won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1954.

directions: Bred by Arlow Stout and introduced in 1935, Dauntless bears warm cantaloupe-orange flowers with unusually wide, overlapping segments for its era, a broader, flatter form that departed from the narrow, trumpet-shaped blooms typical of earlier daylily hybrids and helped set the template for twentieth-century breeding. Its influence on the genus was formally recognized when it received the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1954, two decades after its introduction. The vigorous clumps produce well-branched scapes over a dependable midsummer season and have kept the cultivar in circulation among heirloom daylily collectors ever since. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain strong bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Stout Silver Medal Winners
New York Botanical Garden — Arlow Stout Daylily Research Archives

common_name: Theron Daylily (Historic First Dark Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in 1934 by Arlow Stout after four generations of crosses involving Hemerocallis fulva 'Europa' and H. thunbergii, Theron was the first daylily bred with true dark mahogany-red coloring and became a key parent behind later red cultivars.

directions: Introduced in 1934 by Arlow Stout following four generations of deliberate crossing involving Hemerocallis fulva 'Europa', H. thunbergii, and other species parents, Theron holds a milestone place in daylily history as the first cultivar bred with genuinely dark, mahogany-red petals set against a pale yellow-orange throat, so intensely colored that newly opened flowers can look almost black or purplish in low light. That breakthrough made Theron a foundational parent behind the modern lineage of red daylilies that followed over the next several decades. The three-foot clumps bloom reliably through the midsummer season and have remained sought after by heirloom collectors for their historic significance. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Ophir Daylily (Historic Tall Fragrant Golden Trumpet Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; introduced in 1924 by nurseryman Bertrand Farr and bred in part from the fragrant species Hemerocallis citrina, Ophir is an unusually tall heirloom cultivar prized for its large, sweetly scented, golden-orange trumpet flowers.

directions: Introduced in 1924 by Pennsylvania nurseryman Bertrand Farr and bred in part from the fragrant species Hemerocallis citrina, Ophir stands out among early daylily cultivars for its exceptional height, sending up scapes to four feet or more topped with large, trumpet-shaped, golden-orange flowers reminiscent of an Easter lily. The blooms carry a light, pleasant fragrance inherited from its citrina parentage and open in a heavy, sustained flush beginning in late June that continues for nearly a month, later than many earlier-blooming daylilies. Its combination of height, scent, and floriferousness kept it in commercial circulation for decades and it remains valued today as an authentic early-twentieth-century heirloom. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, siting it toward the back of a border where its height can be appreciated, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database
